body.heading: The experiment, not the exam
paragraphs: The 50/30/20 idea suggests dividing take-home pay into roughly 50% needs, 30% wants, and 20% savings. Instead of trying to obey it forever, run it as an experiment for a single month and simply observe.

On take-home pay of $1,600, the guideline shape would be about $800 for needs, $480 for wants, and $320 for savings. Your real numbers will differ — that difference is the interesting part, not a failure.

body.heading: Sort first, judge later
paragraphs: Spend the month normally, then sort everything you spent into the three buckets. Needs keep life running: housing, bills, basic food, transport, minimum payments. Wants make life nicer. Savings are anything sent to your future.
Most people find the experiment reveals one clear thing: a want that quietly grew teeth, or a need — like a phone contract — that could be renegotiated at renewal. One insight per month is plenty.

body.heading: Adjust the shape, keep the habit
paragraphs: In an expensive city, needs might honestly take 70%. The useful response is not guilt but design: protect a small savings slice first, even 5%, and let the wants bucket flex. A shape you can keep beats a perfect shape you abandon.

Repeat the experiment once or twice a year. Your shape changes as rent, work, and life change, and each run of the experiment updates the map — which is all a budget ever is: a map of where the money goes, drawn honestly.

takeaway: Run 50/30/20 as a one-month experiment, learn what your real shape is, and adjust it gently rather than grading yourself against it.
